---
title: "Using trendspull from R"
output: html_document
---

The native R package returns data frames and matrices and draws ggplot figures.
Requires R 4.1+; Python is not required. Install from the repository using the
instructions in the [README](../README.md#install), then load the package:

```{r library}
library(trendspull)
```

```{r collect, eval=FALSE}
# Step 1: Collect all dates for one geography.
data <- pull_trends(
  c("wildfire", "smoke", "air quality", "asthma", "inhaler", "cough"),
  start = "2021-01-01", end = "2025-12-31", geo = "US-CA"
)
head(data[c("date", "keyword", "value", "calibrated_value")])

# Step 2: Transform to terms-by-weeks proportions.
proportions <- selected_proportions(data)
proportions[, 1:3, drop = FALSE]

# Plot the collected interest on one common 0–100 display scale.
figure <- plot_trends(data)
ggplot2::ggsave("trends.pdf", figure, width = 11, height = 9.5,
                device = grDevices::cairo_pdf)
```

`pull_trends()` returns a data frame with one row per date, term and geography.
Up to five keywords share a raw Google comparison; larger sets automatically use
G-TAB and add `calibrated_value` and conditional rounding bounds. Raw `value`,
zeros and missing quality flags are preserved. The rounding bounds do not cover
Google's sampling variability. See the [data contract](data-contract.md).

`selected_proportions()` returns a numeric matrix whose columns sum to 1 among
the selected terms. `plot_trends()` returns a ggplot/patchwork object with an
overview and individual panels; it uses one maximum across all supplied terms
and dates for its 0–100 display scale. Neither helper changes the collected data.
Select one geography before using either helper, for example
`selected_proportions(data[data$geo == "US-CA", ])`.

Pass `min_gap_days = 28` to keep timestamps at least 28 elapsed days apart;
omitting it keeps every date. Spacing does not guarantee independence. Integer
options accept whole R numbers without an `L` suffix and reject fractional values.
Dates are POSIXct timestamps; use `format(data$date, tz = "UTC")` for UTC labels.

Collection metadata are retained automatically in `attr(data, "trendspull")`.
The helpers require that attribute. Keep it when subsetting, and use RDS to save
the full R object:

```{r save, eval=FALSE}
saveRDS(data, "trends.rds")
data <- readRDS("trends.rds")
```

`write.csv()` exports the columns but loses the metadata attribute. For raw Google
responses and checksums, pass `archive = "data"` to `pull_trends()`; each collection
writes a new run directory, including dates omitted by `min_gap_days`.
